title: The Election Commission of India must end its method of deleting first and verifying later
content_html:
Not one eligible elector should be left out of the electoral rolls. This statement appears in nearly every document released by the Election Commission of India (ECI) as part of the ongoing SIR process, and the Supreme Court of India, which is hearing petitions challenging the SIR, has also used this refrain. Yet, according to an ECI counter-affidavit filed in the Court, by early September 2026, out of more than 38 lakh appeals submitted to SIR appellate tribunals in West Bengal, just over 1,22,000 appeals were disposed of (a disposal rate of just 3.2%) and 1,13,943 electors were added back to the rolls (an inclusion rate of nearly 93%). This suggests that the claims/corrections phase in the West Bengal SIR — during which judicial officers deployed for verification deemed 27 lakh of the 60 lakh electors flagged for “logical discrepancies” to be ineligible — was deeply flawed. More than 22 lakh of those found ineligible have since appealed, and ECI data show that more than nine in 10 cases decided by the tribunals have ended with the electors back on the rolls. If these “inclusion” and “disposal” rates hold, the majority of the 27 lakh electors should not have been ineligible in the first place and are now struggling to get back on the rolls — an indication that massive disenfranchisement preceded the West Bengal Assembly polls. With municipal elections in the State approaching, the ECI must speed up the appellate process and restore eligible electors to the rolls.

In Phase 3 of the SIR, The Hindu’s analysis found that in 24 out of Delhi’s 70 constituencies, the draft roll now records fewer electors than those who voted in the February 2025 Assembly election. Such large-scale deletion cannot hold unless there was a major migration process in the capital region or large numbers of voters were never ordinarily resident in Delhi. A more plausible answer is that the enumeration itself has struck off actual voters. The process puts the onus of proving eligibility on the elector, and the ECI’s dropping of enumeration forms at homes has not translated into full enumeration. Requiring electors to link themselves to rolls drawn in the early 2000s then manufactures “discrepancies” even when documents are valid. In Delhi, this “mapping” has put 13.79 lakh electors under notice with a further 19.33 lakh flagged for “logical discrepancies” on undefined grounds. While hearing the Bihar SIR petitions, the Court had intervened sharply to stop eligible voters from being struck off. Its permissiveness in the year since, towards an insouciant ECI has allowed disenfranchisement on a scale that will remain a black mark on the jurisprudence of universal adult franchise in India. As the Court hears petitions on Delhi and West Bengal, it must compel the ECI to reverse course.

title: Deployment of weapons calls for multilateral governance in space
content_html:
Although the U.S. military doctrine was openly considering offensive and defensive space control by 2025, the admission on September 14 by U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink, and confirmed by Space Force chief Gen. Douglas Schiess, that the country has deployed “on-orbit space control weapons” to “defend against hostile adversary action” is cause for concern. Satellite systems increasingly underpin communications, energy, and financial networks and many commercial systems serve civilian and military users. To that end, the U.S., Russia, China, and India, among others, have been developing counter-space capabilities while contributing to the technological and strategic environment rendering earth orbit the next major battlefield. The increasing military use of commercial satellites can endanger the protections they enjoy under international humanitarian law even as this law is underprepared for satellites being highly interconnected and often dual-use. That said, the details that justify the need for orbital defence systems also make poorly specified weapons a potential cause of instability. Mr. Meink described the weapon as defensive, but U.S. military doctrine defines “space control” as encompassing both offensive and defensive operations.

Compounding the consequences of confusion when two steerable satellites approach each other without understanding the other’s intentions — including due to future autonomous satellites running artificial intelligence models onboard — is the lack of policy details. What constitutes “hostile action” and what the weapon can do remain unclear. While the Outer Space Treaty does not ban weapons in orbit per se, Article IV prohibits nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit — a fluid line considering the centrality of satellite-based networks for contemporary society and the ability of conventional weapons to render damage en masse; its Article III also requires space activities to comply with international law. But when an autonomous, dual-use orbital asset operated by a commercial entity initiates an unwanted defensive strike, the existing rules, including the Liability Convention, cannot be applied straightforwardly to determine accountability. The rules have become too coarse for what contemporary technologies, and the declining esteem for a rules-based world order, warrant. The U.N. Open-Ended Working Group on the ‘Prevention of an Arms Race in Outer Space’ should offer governments an opportunity to address the disclosure. The U.S. government should also reveal the particulars of the weapons it has deployed, and enter into a multilateral governance arrangement that defines exact thresholds of action and escalation.

title: The Koran and politics of purdah
author: A. Faizur Rahman
content_html:
Recently, Kanthapuram A.P. Aboobacker Musliar of the Samastha Kerala Jamiyyathul Ulama issued a circular directing public halls and madrasas not to permit women to share public spaces with unrelated men during religious events.

He subsequently sought to justify the restriction with the startling claim that bringing women onto public platforms would cause “great destruction.” He attributed this danger to the mixing of men and women and said that the Koran itself requires women to remain confined to their homes and prohibits them from appearing in public.

But the Koran does not instruct women to remain confined to their homes. It is conservative clerics who have historically sought to impose such restrictions by taking out of context the instruction in verse 33:33 to “stay in your houses” (qarna fi buyootikunna) and “do not display yourselves as was the display of the former times of ignorance.”

Related Stories

  • Kanthapuram says will defend Shariat laws no matter whoever opposes it

  • Kanthapuram clarifies remarks on women amid criticism

  • Kanthapuram calls for restraint amid protests over remarks on women’s participation

  • CPI(M) general secretary M.A. Baby slams Islamic scholar Kanthapuram’s anti-women remarks

  • Row over Kanthapuram directive limiting women’s public participation grows as Samastha defends ‘right to preach’

Yet the verse occurs within a passage beginning at verse 28 that is explicitly addressed to the Prophet’s wives wherein the Prophet is instructed to give them a choice: they may seek the comforts and adornments of worldly life, in which case they will be granted a gracious separation, or they may choose Allah, the Prophet and the hereafter, for which they will receive a great reward. Their position is then expressly distinguished from that of other women. “O wives of the Prophet, you are not like other women,” verse 32 says, before laying down a heightened standard of conduct for them: the punishment for serious wrongdoing would be doubled, while the reward for righteousness would also be doubled.

The Prophet’s wives are then told to avoid overly soft speech with men, to remain in their houses, not to display themselves as women did in the pre-Islamic period, and to follow Allah and the Prophet. The passage culminates in a reference intended to keep the Prophet’s household spiritually pure.

As is clear from the passage itself, the command to “remain in your houses” is addressed to women whom the Koran explicitly distinguishes from other women saying “you are not like other women.” To remove this instruction from its specific context and present it as a universal Koranic command requiring all Muslim women to remain at home is to extend the verse beyond the scope stated in the passage itself.

Moreover, the historical record does not support the idea that Islam required women to be confined to their homes or excluded from public life. Hazrat Khadija, the Prophet’s first wife, was a successful merchant who conducted her own commercial affairs, and the Prophet himself worked for her as a trading agent before their marriage. Even after he became the Prophet, there is no indication that he asked Khadija to abandon her commercial or public life. This shows that the Prophet did not regard a woman’s participation in economic and social life as incompatible with Islam.

The same is true of the Prophet’s wives who lived after the revelation of Koran 33:33. Hazrat Aisha travelled with the Prophet, including on military expeditions and for the Hajj, and later became one of the most important authorities on religion and law in the early Muslim community. Men and women consulted her, and she transmitted a large body of hadith. She also played a public role in the political conflict that culminated in the Battle of the Camel in 656 CE. Hazrat Umm Salama, another wife of the Prophet, was likewise consulted on matters of public and religious significance.

These examples make it difficult to interpret “remain in your houses” in 33:33 as a command of absolute physical confinement. Whatever restrictions it imposed on the Prophet’s wives, the historical record provides little basis for turning it into a universal prohibition against women leaving their homes, participating in public life or sharing public spaces with men. Not surprisingly, in Al-Muhaddithat, the English introduction to his 43-volume Arabic compendium of Muslim women scholars, Mohammad Akram Nadwi rejects the view that Islam is “a human construct, done mainly by men and therefore done to secure advantages for them at the expense of women.”

Nonetheless, the subjugation of women cannot be challenged through reformist rhetoric alone. It requires the Muslim laity to publicly question clerical authority itself, and political leaders to stop lending legitimacy to regressive clerical institutions through high-profile visits and public engagement. The recent meeting of Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim with Mr. Aboobacker in Keralam, illustrates the problem. Such public recognition can embolden male clerics to present patriarchal interpretations as divine commands and discourage Muslims from questioning them. The future of Islam cannot be left to those who claim a monopoly over its interpretation. If Muslims are to progress, the Koran must remain the primary point of reference, while the Prophet’s life must be taken seriously as evidence of how Koranic principles were actually lived.

A. Faizur Rahman is Independent researcher and Secretary-General of the Islamic Forum for the Promotion of Moderate Thought. X: @FaizEngineer

title: Persistent antagonism towards Urdu
author: Shaikh Mujibur Rehman
content_html:
In June 2026, a group of approximately 10-15 men entered Bharat Chandra High School in Armoor, Nizamabad district, Telangana, and allegedly manhandled its 37-year-old Principal, Aamir Khan. The incident reportedly arose from the perception that Urdu was being taught at the school. However, Mr. Khan, an English teacher, was not responsible for teaching Urdu; the subject had been taught briefly by another teacher. The school’s management board, headed by a person of Hindu background, had decided to introduce Urdu as a second language following a request from the parents of Muslim students, who constitute approximately 25% of the school’s total strength.

This episode is particularly significant in light of a Supreme Court judgment in April 2025, which described Urdu as a fine expression of Ganga-Jamuni Tehzeeb. A Bench comprising Justices Sudhanshu Dhulia and Vinod Chandran observed that “language belongs to a community, to a region, to people but not a religion.” The Court upheld the use of Urdu on the signboard of a municipal council in Maharashtra and declined to interfere with the Bombay High Court’s ruling, which had found no legal prohibition under the Maharashtra Local Authorities (Official Languages) Act, 2022, against the use of Urdu.

The contrast between the constitutional-legal recognition of Urdu as a linguistic and cultural tradition and the hostility towards it highlights the contested and communal nature of the language in today’s India.

Related Stories

  • Urdu is the finest specimen of composite cultural ethos of India, says Supreme Court

  • In Uttar Pradesh, a language of loss: the decline of Urdu

  • In Delhi’s Urdu-medium schools, learning, shadowed by neglect

  • Danish Mahal: inside Lucknow’s Urdu landmark

  • Why Urdu is disappearing from classrooms — and who’s trying to save it

  • Once the language of masses, Urdu is dying a slow death

  • Urdu and patriotism

The antagonism towards Urdu is rooted in the perception that it is exclusively a language for Muslims. The establishment of Bangladesh in 1971 around the Bengali language demonstrated that Urdu is not the language of Muslims as a whole. Moreover, Urdu has historically been spoken and cultivated by Hindus, Sikhs, and others. Rakhshanda Jalil’s edited volume, Whose Urdu Is It Anyway?, brings together writings by several prominent non-Muslim literary figures, including Gulzar, Ramanand Sagar, Rajinder Singh Bedi, and Kishan Chander. Their contributions demonstrate how Urdu has historically been embedded within a diverse literary and cultural tradition. A particularly revealing case is that of Rahi Masoom Raza, the author associated with the TV serial Mahabharat. It has recently come to light that his novel Aadha Gaon (Half Village), a classic of modern Hindi literature, was originally written by him in Urdu.

Not all that different

In ordinary discourse, the difference between Hindi and Urdu is not easily noticeable. According to Paul Brass, Urdu, “in its original form, was nothing more grammatically than the spoken Hindustani of north India, particularly Khari Boli of the Delhi area, with an infusion of Persian, Arabic, and Turkish vocabulary.” This shared linguistic heritage highlights the extent to which Hindi and Urdu evolved from a common linguistic base. In 1837, Persian was replaced by English and other vernacular languages in various provinces of British India for administrative and judicial purposes. In north India, however, the vernacular language selected for official use was not Hindi, but Urdu written in the Perso-Arabic script. This linguistic policy subsequently became a source of controversy and led to the emergence of the Hindi movement.

Related Stories

  • Treat Urdu and Sanskrit with equality and respect, Tejashwi Yadav tells Bihar CM

  • Urdu is an Indian language, says Murli Manohar Joshi

Around this period, two publications, one by Babu Shiva Prasad and another by Madan Mohan Malviya, contributed significantly to bolstering the Hindi movement. In 1868, Babu Shiva Prasad published a memorandum on court characters, in which he highlighted the adverse effects of the use of Urdu in the North-Western Provinces and Oudh (administrative province in British India). Similarly, Madan Mohan Malviya’s Court Character and Primary Education in the North-Western Provinces and Oudh expressed concern over the detrimental impact of officially encouraging Urdu among a Hindu population. At the same time, pro-Urdu campaigns also emerged. Thus, the controversy increasingly moved beyond pamphlets and petitions, giving rise to various organised efforts.

In independent India, the Hindi-Urdu controversy continued to be a divisive political issue, particularly in north India. The persistence of antagonism towards Urdu is especially striking in a country where English, a language of foreign origin, continues to be widely valued and institutionalised across regions. In contrast, Urdu, despite its historical and cultural roots in the Indian subcontinent, continues to encounter hostility.

Shaikh Mujibur Rehman is Author of ‘Shikwa-e- Hind:The Political Future of Indian Muslims’. Views are personal

title: A Malacca-Singapore model for resolving Hormuz
author: M. Kalyanaraman
content_html:
As the siege warfare continues in the Strait of Hormuz and the world suffers, it may be instructive to revisit the Straits of Malacca and Singapore.

The Strait of Malacca runs for some 800 kilometres between the Malay Peninsula and the Indonesian island of Sumatra, connecting the Andaman Sea to the Strait of Singapore, while the Strait of Singapore, some 105 km long, forms its eastern continuation and connects the Malacca Strait to the South China Sea.

A territorial turning point

The Straits were once considered “international” in the sense that they were like the high seas, over which no country had any claim. In 1971, Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore jointly challenged this notion.

Indonesia, a newly decolonised nation, feared for the security of its individual islands if the waters between them were not considered its territory, and in 1957 declared that all waters “surrounding, between and connecting the islands” were Indonesian waters. Then Indonesian President Sukarno had an adversarial relationship with the colonial powers, and the nation was wary of big-power interference.

As the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)was being formulated, Indonesia insisted that its territorial waters should extend 12 nautical miles from the outermost islands. The two nations continue to cooperate actively to this day.

  • Singapore backs India’s plan to patrol Malacca Strait

At their narrowest points, the Straits are well under 24 nautical miles wide. Once both states claimed 12-nautical-mile territorial seas, the zones met in the middle, leaving no strip of high seas or exclusive economic zone (EEZ) between them. Under the customary law of the time, this meant that the Straits were simply territorial seas, where foreign vessels enjoyed only the right of “innocent passage” — a right that Indonesia or Malaysia could suspend for security reasons and that excluded submerged submarines.

The three nations issued a joint statement in 1971 proposing a coordinating body comprising representatives of the three states to administer the Straits. Singapore, an island nation dependent on trade and shipping, did not quite agree to declaring the Straits “not international”, but did make common cause with Malaysia over the safety of navigation.

The Straits and the great powers

Japan, a major player through the Japan-funded Malacca Strait Council, offered cooperation with the three states rather than seeking an internationalised regime. The United States and the Soviet Union, otherwise rivals, were allies on this one issue — keeping the Straits under territorial waters “international” so that ships retained the right of “continued, politically uncluttered transit”.

As UNCLOS entered its final phase of formulation in the 1970s, the United Kingdom introduced the concept of “transit passage” for straits connecting the high seas or EEZs — a right of transit only in a “continuous and expeditious” manner, with no stopping or loitering, but one that applied to warships as well, going beyond mere innocent passage. Indonesia agreed to this formulation with reservations, trading its acceptance for greater security for its archipelago, which UNCLOS eventually addressed separately. Malaysia’s concerns centred on environmental safety, insurance requirements and permissible vessel draught.

In 2007, the three states working with the international community arrived at a Cooperative Mechanism building on a traffic separation scheme similar to what Iran and Oman had agreed for the Strait of Hormuz in the 1960s. A core aspect of the 2007 mechanism was for user states and industry to contribute to a fund for aids to navigation, hydrographic surveys and safety projects, administered jointly with the littoral states.

The Aids to Navigation Fund is supported through voluntary financial contributions from non-profit organisations such as The Nippon Foundation and the International Foundation for Aids to Navigation, as well as industry stakeholders and states with an interest in the safe and efficient use of the Straits. These contributions do not amount to tolls. The fund is administered on a rotation basis by a committee comprising representatives of the three littoral States and the contributors. The three littoral States — Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore — do not impose fees, tolls or any other form of payment on ships exercising their right of transit passage.

The geographic parallel

The Strait of Hormuz is similar to the Malacca-Singapore Straits, in that the territorial waters of Iran and Oman intersect, making sections of the Strait part of their territorial waters.

In 1993, Iran, which has not ratified UNCLOS, passed a law requiring foreign warships to seek its authorisation to pass through the Strait. This continues to be a sore point today.

Persian Gulf nations have a history of both conflict and cooperation. The United Arab Emirates, for instance, was among Iran’s leading trading partners. Qatar is among the Persian Gulf nations that have supported the Iran-Oman talks. It had also mooted the Malacca-Singapore straits as a model.

Yet, even if the Gulf nations arrive at a framework they all agree on, the U.S. has shown that it may not accept it. The Malacca-Singapore issue was resolved as UNCLOS itself was being put into effect, when trade-offs were part of negotiating a convention intended to govern the world’s oceans.

A key concern in the Malacca-Singapore Straits was the safety of navigation and the environment, whereas in the Strait of Hormuz, the key issue is Iran’s security.

Iran is demanding that all nations revisit the Strait of Hormuz, and some are willing to do so. Though Iran and Oman have apparently agreed on a framework for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, the Strait has not been reopened, and the U.S. has not accepted the arrangement. The context has changed, even though there are clear parallels in the technical details.

title: Letters to The Editor — September 22, 2026
content_html:
A tussle that distresses

The challenge to the reappointment of N. Chandrasekaran as Chairman of Tata Sons on September 17 is distressing to the company’s stakeholders in particular and to thousands of shareholders in the Indian corporate world in general (Page 1, “Tata Sons Board did not meet conditions: Trusts”, September 21). The reputation and esteem meticulously built over many decades by the Tata brand in the business world are at great risk of erosion because of the impatient and intolerant attitude of the Board of Directors. A quarrel in public is no way to resolve differences among learned, experienced and wise board members. India, known for a paucity of eminent leaders in politics, eagerly looks to the corporate world for wise and pragmatic business leaders who can provide good governance. Individual egos need to be set aside.

M.V. Nagavender Rao,

Hyderabad

Politics and decorum

Even the staunchest critics of Prime Minister Narendra Modi would find it difficult to accept Rahul Gandhi, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, turning an event meant to address the serious issues confronting today’s youth into a vehicle to lampoon the Prime Minister. Using a stand-up comedian to mimic and ridicule Mr. Modi at such an event was unbecoming of the office of the Leader of the Opposition. By encouraging such mimicry, Mr. Gandhi has betrayed a lack of political maturity. A person portrayed by Gandhi family loyalists as a potential Prime Minister is expected to conduct himself with dignity and poise. The Bharatiya Janata Party’s outrage is not misplaced.

S.K. Choudhury,

Bengaluru

The developments remind me of the days when Jawaharlal Nehru was Prime Minister. The celebrated cartoonist K. Shankar often drew cartoons criticising and poking fun at Nehru. Far from taking offence, Nehru reportedly encouraged Shankar to continue criticising him through his cartoons. Whether one agrees with the criticism or not, this reflects an important democratic principle: those in power must be able to tolerate criticism, satire and even ridicule. Freedom of expression is one of the very foundations of a democratic society.

Mohan Nedungadi,

Cherppulassery, Keralam

title: The arithmetic of Tamil Nadu’s growth ambition
author: C. Rangarajan,K.R.  Shanmugam
content_html:
At the NITI Aayog meeting on June 11, 2026, Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay announced the goal of transforming Tamil Nadu into a $1.5 trillion economy by 2035-36. A similar view has also been expressed by others.

Tamil Nadu’s Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP) was ₹35.29 lakh crore in 2025-26. To achieve the target of $1.5 trillion in 10 years, Tamil Nadu would have to increase the size of its economy to ₹172.56 lakh crore by 2035-36, registering a 4.9-fold increase. This calculation is based on the assumption that the exchange rate of one dollar in terms of rupees will appreciate by 2% per annum from its present level, touching ₹115.38 per dollar in 2035-36. This implies that achieving the target would require a nominal growth rate of 17.2% and, assuming inflation of 5%, a real growth rate of 12.2% per annum continuously for 10 years.

title: Serious escalation: On the U.S., Russia Sanctions Act and India
content_html:
The U.S. Russia Sanctions Act, now signed into law by President Donald Trump, and its resultant impending tariffs, present a new and substantially different escalation of tensions between the U.S. and India. The law provides the U.S. President the authority to levy tariffs of up to 100% on countries such as India that import large quantities of Russian oil and gas. This is more serious than the penal tariffs that Mr. Trump had levied earlier. The escalation last year of reciprocal tariffs to 50% on India’s import of Russian oil was based on an Executive Order, and could be rescinded through the same method. This latest Act has been passed by the U.S. Congress and so carries a higher order of legal permanence and authority. Mr. Trump will have to justify in writing to Congress any waiver he wants to provide. The 50% tariffs hit Indian exports to the U.S. hard, but the impact was somewhat mitigated by exporters sharing the cost with their American customers. That was, however, a financially devastating and unsustainable bid to retain customers. Sharing a 100% tariff will be impossible for India’s largely micro, small and medium enterprises (MSME) exporters. The 100% tariffs are also over and above the 10% ‘forced labour’ tariffs and the 50% Section 232 tariffs on steel and aluminium. Indian exports to the U.S. will simply become too uncompetitive should these new tariffs come to pass. India has three options before it: cut Russian oil imports, retain those imports and bear the tariffs, or convince the U.S. to implement a low tariff using the “up to 100%” phrasing of the law.

Continuing with Russian oil imports and bearing the tariffs would be a significant blow to India’s export ambitions and MSMEs. The U.S. is India’s largest export destination, accounting for about 20% of its total goods exports. In any case, historical data have shown that India has usually complied with U.S. pressure to cut oil imports from particular countries, including from Russia, vocal claims of strategic autonomy aside. Finding other sources will be difficult. Russia accounted for more than 51% of India’s oil imports as of July 2026, while supplies through the Strait of Hormuz remain constrained. India will have to chivvy countries such as Oman to hasten their expansion of alternative ports. The price of oil remains well above $100 a barrel, meaning finding favourable deals with new suppliers will be increasingly difficult. Union Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal will have much to do during his planned trip to the U.S. at the end of this month for the G-20 Trade Ministerial. There are still 30 days before the U.S. can levy its tariffs. India’s ability to secure a low rate will be a true test of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s friendship with Mr. Trump.

title: Antidote to drugs: On the counterfeit medicine racket in Bengaluru, Karnataka
content_html:
With the recent bust of a counterfeit medicine racket in Bengaluru, a public policy issue with broad ramifications for health care in the State has emerged. Centered around Bengaluru, relabelled or fake drugs, including cancer drugs, injections used in the ICU, were supplied to more than 90 hospitals and clinics across the State. The lid was blown off this elaborate scam after incidental raids, near Bidadi in Karnataka on August 18, found suspected fake drugs and expired drugs at a farmhouse which was an unlicensed unit. The consignment had a label value of ₹5 crore. Investigators said that the farmhouse was used in an illicit drug operation — involving the repacking of fake and expired drugs as fresh consignments, with altered expiry dates, and as expensive, imported branded drugs — which were then sold at massive discounts. The State later formed a Special Investigation Team to trace the wider network. While exploring the distribution mechanism, investigators found that the network had been supplying these drugs to over 90 hospitals in the State, in cahoots with a pharmacy in Bengaluru, indicating that a network was thriving well before the bust. A few persons have been arrested and the police are on the tail of another who is not in the country at present. The impunity with which the scamsters were operating is an indication of the unreliable scrutiny of the quality of drugs in the market. The biggest concern, however, is patient safety, given that these are drugs that can save lives and are marked out for time-sensitive usage. Also being examined are possible inter-State links, as investigators have launched a complete review of the supply chain. The illicit channels through which private hospitals bought and used these drugs, including possible complicity in the private hospital network, are under scrutiny.

With alarming regularity, issues to do with poor quality, spurious, fake or expired drugs hit the headlines in India. For a nation that zealously aspires to become the ‘pharmacy of the world’, India struggles to match its ambition with adequate and stringent monitoring and quality control systems. The question of drug quality is particularly significant as fake or spurious drugs can cause immediate adverse reactions, lead to severe disabilities, and even death. Recent incidents of contaminated cough syrups causing deaths, not only in India, but across the world, have further highlighted these woefully inadequate systems and consistently dented the pride of the “Make in India” campaign. Irrespective of whether India becomes the pharmacy of the world, there is a pressing need to make sure that drugs and medical supplies made in the country fulfil the highest quality standards.
